# Data Processing

## Core ideas and reasoning

Data processing converts raw facts into useful results through collection, preparation, input, processing, output and storage. Validation checks whether data meet rules, such as a permitted range, data type, presence or format. Verification checks that entered data match the source, for example by double entry or proofreading. A valid value can still be incorrect: a score of 65 passes a 0–100 range check even if the source says 56. Batch processing groups transactions for later processing; real-time processing responds within the timing requirements of a task. In a spreadsheet formulas start with =, functions have names and arguments, and cell references can be relative, absolute or mixed. Copying =A1+B1 down one row changes it to =A2+B2; $A$1 fixes both parts. Sorting changes record order while filtering displays records meeting conditions. Computational errors include overflow beyond the representable range, truncation from discarding digits, and rounding from approximating values. Keep original precision when possible and round final outputs according to purpose.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Distinguish validation and verification with an example.

Validation could check a mark is between 0 and 100. Verification compares the entered mark with the source. A value can pass validation yet be a copying error.

### Example 2

A formula =$A$1*B2 is copied from C2 to C3. State the new formula.

=$A$1*B3. The absolute reference remains fixed and the relative reference moves down one row.

### Example 3

Distinguish sorting from filtering.

Sorting arranges records in an order such as ascending surname. Filtering displays records meeting criteria while hiding the others without deleting them.

### Example 4

Distinguish between text wrap and word wrap in word processing.

Text wrap arranges text around an inserted object. Word wrap automatically moves text to the next line when it reaches the margin.

### Example 5

Distinguish first-line indentation from hanging indentation.

A first-line indent shifts the first line of a paragraph. A hanging indent shifts the remaining lines while the first line stays farther left.

### Example 6

Identify the elements of a spreadsheet function.

An equals sign, function name and arguments, with the arguments enclosed in parentheses; for example =SUM(A1:A3).

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
